catalog_quote: 3.3 アクセント アクセントは高低アクセントで、平板、高低、低高、高低低、低高低、低低高が現れる。異なるアクセントは許容されないので、弁別的に機能しているものと思われる。音節数が増えてくると、平板タイプはずっと現れるけれども、現時点では低高高や高高低のように高が一部続くタイプは観察できなかった。なお高低高のように一単語内に二度高い位置が現れることは決してないので、単語アクセントが頂点表示機能を持つといえる。以下のアクセント表記は、高のみ記号を付与して、低には付与していないことを申し添える。 [p.48: 2音節語 úté, "breast": 13 (平板) / kárbo, "eye": 5 (高低) / ʃubó, "head": 1 (低高); 3音節語 móógú, "egg": 61 (平板) / mánik'e, "spit": 12 (高低低) / podoró, "lip": 10 (低低高) / koʃólgu, "elbow": 29 (低高低)] [p.49: 先行研究と比較した場合、全く同じ単語で異なるアクセントタイプが確認できるので、方言差があるのか、それともアクセント自体どの程度弁別的に機能しているかは今後の課題である。 rúwa (Galgida) / rúá (Kuchur), "body": 47; podoró (Galgida) / pódoro (Kuchur), "lip": 10]

new_statements.translation: 3.3 Accent. The accent is a pitch (high-low) accent; level [all-high], HL, LH, HLL, LHL and LLH occur. Since a different accent [on a given word] is not accepted, it appears to function distinctively. As the number of syllables increases the level type keeps appearing, but so far types in which the high continues over part of the word, such as LHH or HHL, could not be observed. Moreover, a high never appears in two positions within one word, as in HLH, so the word accent can be said to have a culminative (peak-marking) function. Note that in the accent transcription below only High is marked and Low is left unmarked.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (24 pp., Acrobat paper-capture scan; scanned text garbled, so I rendered pp.7-9 = journal pp.47-49 at 150 dpi and read the page scan). Section '3.3 アクセント' is at the bottom of p.47 exactly as quoted: 'アクセントは高低アクセントで、平板、高低、低高、高低低、低高低、低低高が現れる。異なるアクセントは許容されないので、弁別的に機能しているものと思われる。音節数が増えてくると、平板タイプはずっと現れるけれども、現時点では低高高や高高低のように高が一部続くタイプは観察できなかった。なお高低高のように一単語内に二度高い位置が現れることは決してないので、単語アクセントが頂点表示機能を持つといえる。以下のアクセント表記は、高のみ記号を付与して、低には付与していないことを申し添える。' -- character-for-character match with the report's quote. The bracketed example list is a faithful condensation of p.48 (source gives item numbers too: úté 'breast' :13 (平板), kárbo 'eye' :5 (高低), ʃubó 'head' :1 (低高); móógú 'egg' :61 (平板), mánik'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prosody analysed as a culminative pitch accent: each word is either 'level' (all syllables high) or has exactly one high-pitched syllable, whose position (1st, 2nd or 3rd syllable) is lexically specified and contrastive; no word has two separate highs. No stress distinct from this pitch accent is described.
new_statements.exceptions: p.48-49: in vowel sequences and long vowels the pitch may rise or fall within the sequence (muólu 'shadow', kíem 'one', boólu 'ash', gúu 'fire'), leaving the diphthong/long-vowel analysis open; p.49: identical words show different accent types from Hieda's (1991) Kuchur-village data (rúwa vs rúá 'body', podoró vs pódoro 'lip'), so whether this is dialectal or reflects limited distinctiveness of accent is left for future work. Hieda 1992 §2.3 instead speaks of two tones (H, L) whose functions are 'not yet sufficiently investigated' and does not describe them.
new_statements.domain_note: Elicited citation forms of nouns (2- and 3-syllable words from a questionnaire wordlist), single 18-year-old speaker from Galgida village; word-level accent only, no phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: Inui 2011 describes the 'Galgida dialect' of Kowegu (ガルギダ村, Nyangatom zone), one 18-year-old speaker, and explicitly notes differences (including accent placement on identical words) from Hieda's 'Koegu' of Kuchur village (= Muguji, lower Omo). Both are the southern Koegu/Muguji variety of ISO xwg / kweg1241; neither source covers the northern Kwegu (Yidinit/Nyidi) spoken among the Mursi and Bodi. Hieda 1992 treats Koegu prosody as two-level tone (undescribed); Inui 2011 analyses it as culminative pitch accent.

sources.note: Sec. 3.3 'アクセント' (p.47-49): word prosody is a pitch (high-low) accent; attested patterns level(all-H), HL, LH, HLL, LHL, LLH; never two separate H positions in a word, so word accent is culminative; position differs lexically (kárbo 'eye' HL vs ʃubó 'head' LH; mánik'e HLL, koʃólgu LHL, podoró LLH); same words show different accent types from Hieda's Kuchur data, so dialect difference / degree of distinctiveness left open. No separate 'stress' notion.
No prosodic features (13A-17A) coded for Koegu; only 116A.
